title: Geospatial assessment of rooftop solar photovoltaic potential for university campus decarbonization in hot-arid environments
abstract: University campuses in hot-arid environments combine high solar irradiance, large underutilized rooftop areas, and cooling-dominated electricity demand that align closely with peak solar generation. Yet campus-scale assessments in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region remain scarce, and existing studies rarely integrate actual building-level electricity consumption, including parking shade structures as co-equal deployment surfaces, or apply multiregional input–output lifecycle carbon accounting. This study addresses all three gaps through a geospatial assessment of rooftop and parking-lot solar photovoltaic potential at Qatar University, combining high-resolution LiDAR-derived digital surface models with six years of building-level electricity consumption data. Solar radiation modeling in ArcGIS Pro with slope, aspect, and irradiance threshold filtering identified 21 suitable buildings and their associated parking canopy structures. Photovoltaic performance was modeled using temperature-corrected efficiency at 22% for monocrystalline silicon modules, a performance ratio of 0.86, and Qatar-specific climatic parameters. Campus-wide deployment could generate 330,587 kWh annually, split between building rooftops (58%) and parking canopy structures (42%), against a total campus demand of 318,184 kWh, yielding a Campus Self-Sufficiency Ratio of approximately 103.8%. Nine buildings achieve self-sufficiency ratios above 80%, with several reaching net-positive annual energy status. Direct operational CO 2 emissions are avoided, totalling approximately 144.8 tonnes annually. MRIO lifecycle analysis using the EXIOBASE 3 database yields a net carbon footprint reduction of 0.475 kg CO 2 -eq/kWh and a campus-wide lifecycle reduction of approximately 157.0 tonnes CO 2 -eq annually, equivalent to the sequestration of approximately 6,652 mature trees. Eleven high-priority buildings achieve 6 to 7-year payback periods under cost-reflective pricing. These findings provide a replicable framework for institutional decarbonization in hot-arid regions where dust accumulation, temperature-induced efficiency losses, and cooling-driven demand patterns differ fundamentally from temperate contexts.

title: Controlled-Memory Identification with Shared Generators: Dimension--Horizon Tradeoffs and Quantum--Classical Separation
abstract: We determine the finite-horizon identification limits of a \(d\)-dimensional memory when the control interface is restricted to four shared, time-homogeneous generators. A writer encodes a message by applying a prefix word to a common root state. The verifier then applies a candidate-dependent query word followed by a shared terminal binary test, with each word of length at most \(T\). For fixed error tolerances \(λ_2>0\) and \(λ_1+λ_2<1\), the optimal identification sizes satisfy \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d^2,T\})\) for arbitrary CPTP generators and \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ_{λ_1,λ_2}(\min\{d,T\})\) for stochastic maps. Four unitary letters and four permutation letters attain these respective bounds, showing that a four-letter reversible alphabet reaches the static code-size orders in optimal quadratic and linear word length. In the fully dimension-limited regime, this yields \(\ln N_{\mathsf Q,4}=Θ(d^2)\) versus \(\ln N_{\mathsf S,4}=Θ(d)\), establishing a quadratic quantum--classical separation in logarithmic code size. Low-overlap Grassmann and agreement-code packings supply the orbit endpoints, while exact inverse query words match each encoded state to its designated test. At the sharp boundary \(λ_2=0\), \(0\leqλ_1<1\), all four model classes satisfy \(\ln N=Θ(\min\{\ln d,T\})\). Thus any fixed positive false-acceptance tolerance activates the metric-packing regime, whereas zero false acceptance imposes an exclusive-witness constraint and yields the logarithmic-dimension boundary.

title: Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.

title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation
abstract: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM's generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.

title: Decoupled Safety Control: A Safety-Control Algorithm for Training-Free Safety Guidance
abstract: Diffusion models achieve strong performance in text-to-image generation, but they can still produce unsafe content. Training-free safety guidance offers a practical inference-time alternative that intervenes during sampling without modifying model weights. However, many existing safeguards still rely on a coupled safety-control chain. In this chain, the same unsafe condition simultaneously specifies what should be avoided, indicates the current unsafe signal, constructs the intervention, and determines when that intervention remains active. This coupling can work when unsafe factors are explicit, but becomes less reliable once harmful and benign semantics are entangled in the current generation state, often leaving residual unsafe content or unnecessarily degrading benign-generation quality or prompt fidelity. We address this problem with Decoupled Safety Control (DSC), a plug-in safety-control algorithm for training-free safety guidance. DSC reformulates training-free safety guidance as an explicit state-dependent control process, so the executed intervention is determined from the current generation state rather than inherited directly from a single unsafe condition. Experiments on standard safety benchmarks show that DSC improves representative latent- and text-space safeguards, achieving stronger unsafe-content suppression while preserving benign-generation quality and maintaining efficient inference.

title: All-in-One Memory: Process-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Memory Agents
abstract: Large language models increasingly rely on external memory to answer queries grounded in long-horizon histories such as multi-session dialogues and lengthy documents. However, existing memory methods often optimize retrieval and memory construction separately, without a shared reward space for evaluating search, writing, and stopping decisions. To address this, we propose All-in-One Memory (AiO-Mem), which organizes these operations as transitions over a shared evidence state and directly evaluates the semantic quality of each action in a unified reward space. AiO-Mem compiles heterogeneous histories into source-traceable multi-view events, providing a shared substrate for retrieval and memory writing. A unified memory policy actor then rolls out complete interaction trajectories over this shared evidence state. A separate trajectory-conditioned process reward model is trained through evidence-grounded supervised fine-tuning and trajectory-level DPO to assign process scores to the collected trajectories. These scores are aggregated into an action-balanced trajectory reward and used by Process-Aligned DAPO (PA-DAPO) to optimize the memory policy. Across long-context memory benchmarks, AiO-Mem consistently improves answer accuracy over both static memory systems and RL-trained memory agents.

title: A Quantum Machine Learning Approach to Content-Based Media Recommendation
abstract: We use quantum machine learning techniques to develop a content-based media recommender system and evaluate its performance on TV programmes using textual descriptions from one week of BBC iPlayer data. Grounded in the Quantum Natural Language Processing framework (QNLP), programme synopses are mapped to variational quantum circuits using their semantic structure. The parameters of these circuits are trained via a supervised pairwise similarity learning task. We benchmark the quantum recommender against a classical BiLSTM baseline trained on the same dataset and objective. While both models achieve comparable performance on the similarity learning task, the quantum model requires significantly fewer parameters (47k vs. 17.8M). When the BiLSTM is constrained to a matching parameter budget, its performance degrades substantially (by 3.63 percentage points in Mean Average Precision (MAP)), indicating that the structured quantum representation provides a highly parameter-efficient alternative in this setting. We demonstrate the feasibility of executing the trained models on quantum hardware by deploying the circuits on Quantinuum's System Model H2 (and accompanying emulator) using a SWAP-test-based protocol. The results confirm that the similarity signal is preserved under realistic, noisy conditions. Taken together, these findings highlight the potential of variational quantum circuits for recommendation tasks and represent a practical step toward their real-world deployment.

title: When do quantum views help? Complementary classical-quantum representations in multi-view fusion
abstract: Recent studies have reported promising results from quantum machine learning in drug discovery, healthcare, materials science and cybersecurity. Research includes comparisons with classical machine learning algorithms and the development of sequential hybrid pipelines. We propose that fusion can improve prediction when classical and quantum representations capture complementary predictive relationships. Our classical-quantum multi-view framework preserves the full classical input alongside simulated quantum features. Concatenation and attention combine the views; single-view comparisons, replacement and masking controls assess both views' contributions. Controlled angular-polynomial experiments distinguish targets adequately represented by a single view from those that depend on complementary angular and polynomial relationships. For these mixed targets, fusion improves prediction by combining the relevant feature sets, while matched classical representations recover the same benefit, linking the improvement to their complementary predictive content. Controlled classification tests further show that gains depend on alignment between the chosen representation and the target, and on a suitable fusion rule. Benchmark validation shows improved mean predictive performance over classical baselines on Wine, Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer, three-class Fashion-MNIST and Steel Plates Faults within the evaluated protocols. Classical replacement and masking controls remain competitive, classical baselines lead on Digits and Covertype, and outcomes with missing or corrupted views depend on the available inputs. These findings support evaluating quantum representations for their complementary predictive contribution and matching the representation and fusion strategy to the target relationships.

title: Solar Decomp consistency study: analysis scripts and derived data
abstract: Analysis scripts and derived data behind a study of how consistent the Erbs, Reindl-2 and DIRINT decomposition models are with the DNI and DHI fields of IWEC2 weather files for Argentina, with a limited comparison against ground measurements (BSRN, SURFRAD, SRRL and the INAHE station in Mendoza). Includes the one-minute global and diffuse series of the INAHE station in Mendoza (2022-2025). The IWEC2 files and the BSRN, SURFRAD and SRRL series are not redistributed; file lists and hashes are provided.

title: EL-RAKHAWI DOCTRINE FOR NEURO-SYMBOLIC OPEN SCIENCE INTELLIGENCE A Unified Framework for Environmental Monitoring, Computer Vision, and Drug Discovery
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Doctrine for Neuro-Symbolic Open Science Intelligence (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23394614) introduces a groundbreaking unified framework (ER-OSI) that bridges fragmented scientific domains—computer vision (INSAIT), long-term ecological monitoring (LTER-BG, Black Sea oceanography), and molecular drug discovery (IMB-BAS)—under a single, logically verifiable Open Science infrastructure. Standard AI applications in Open Science suffer from "context poisoning" and algorithmic hallucination when synthesizing cross-disciplinary data. This framework embeds a Neuro-Symbolic Verification Engine within the Open Science pipeline, mapping retrieved scientific data to a structured Eco-Biomedical Knowledge Graph and applying First-Order Logic consistency checks before generative models process the information. Central to this doctrine is the Open Science Reliability Index (OSRI) = (D_q × S_v × C_o) / ((D_q × S_v × C_o) + (W × H_r × B_d) + 0.01), with W=10, mathematically proving that massive data volume cannot compensate for logical inconsistency or scientific bias. Simulated validation demonstrates an 80% reduction in hallucination rates compared to baseline AI pipelines, while inherently defending against scientific misinformation. Aligned with the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC) and Bulgarian Open Science Portal (BPOS) initiatives, the framework transforms AI-driven discovery from a "black box" to an auditable "glass box." Protected under sovereign intellectual property with explicit prohibitions against unauthorized AI training ingestion or commercial exploitation. All moral, financial, academic, and proprietary rights are exclusively reserved to Dr. Mohamed Kamal Arafa El-Rakhawi—establishing a scientifically rigorous, transparent, and truly responsible pathway for the future of global Open Science.

title: Adaptive Self-Reinforcement and Mutual Reinforcement in Self-and-Interactive Models: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Switching Between Independent and Relational Improvement
abstract: Models and computational systems can improve through internal processes or through interactions with other models and systems. However, these two modes of improvement are often investigated under different assumptions, objectives, and methodological frameworks. This paper proposes Adaptive Self-and-Mutual Reinforcement (ASMR), a conceptual framework for coordinating self-reinforcement and mutual reinforcement within a higher-level class of models termed Self-and-Interactive Models (SIMs). The proposed framework is not restricted to large language models, artificial intelligence agents, or any specific computational architecture. Instead, it treats independent improvement and relational improvement as general mechanisms through which models can modify their internal states, capabilities, strategies, representations, or operating configurations. The central principle is that a model should not be permanently restricted to either independent improvement or interaction-dependent improvement. Rather, it should adaptively select, alternate between, combine, or temporarily suspend these mechanisms according to their expected marginal benefits, costs, uncertainty, reliability, and effects on the overall system. The framework formalizes self-reinforcement, mutual reinforcement, reinforcement-mode selection, transition control, and feedback-based adaptation. It also identifies potential failure modes, including self-reinforcing errors, negative interaction cycles, redundant mutual feedback, excessive switching, and collective degradation. A research agenda is proposed to compare adaptive switching with self-only, mutual-only, fixed-hybrid, and randomly switching baselines. This paper establishes a conceptual and mathematical foundation for investigation; it does not claim that the proposed framework has already demonstrated empirical superiority or that its complete novelty has been established.

title: The Impact of Earthquake Early Warning Systems on Smart Cities' Resilience: Conceptual Framework and Comprehensive Review
abstract: Earthquake Early Warning Systems (EEWS) are critical components of resilient smart cities, employing advanced digital technologies to reduce the impacts of seismic events and strengthen urban disaster preparedness. These systems integrate distributed Internet of Things (IoT) devices, wireless sensor networks, high-speed communication infrastructures, and machine learning algorithms to detect, analyze, and evaluate seismic activity in real time. Data collected from interconnected ground-motion sensors are rapidly transmitted to processing centers, enabling the estimation of earthquake magnitude, location, and expected intensity before strong ground shaking reaches affected areas. When integrated into smart urban infrastructures, EEWS can trigger automated and coordinated responses, including halting public transportation, controlling elevators, isolating critical power and gas networks, protecting vulnerable infrastructure, and initiating emergency communication protocols. This study examines the integration of EEWS into smart city frameworks, focusing on their role in enhancing disaster preparedness, real-time decision-making, and adaptive urban governance. It also discusses technological, operational, organizational, and institutional challenges, including data interoperability, communication reliability, system maintenance, and coordination among stakeholders. By embedding EEWS within interconnected urban systems, the study highlights their potential to enhance public safety, reduce socioeconomic disruption, and support the development of adaptive and earthquake-resilient urban environments.

title: RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary
abstract: Weight quantization below four bits shrinks memory and bandwidth at a perplexity that looks acceptable, but often at the cost of factual knowledge and task accuracy. Ternary weights have mostly been obtained by training from scratch or long fine-tuning. We introduce RoleQ, a quantization framework that places scales by the functional roles of Transformer units rather than by the layout of the weight matrix, as conventional formats do. Vectors that read from the residual stream take one scale per output unit; those that write to it, one per input unit. The rule is structural, needs no search, calibration or stored state, and holds on integer and ternary grids. In a rotated basis it matches a per-layer axis search at half the solver work, and at ternary it cuts perplexity by up to half against layout-based placement in two families at every size from 0.6B to 14B, where per-row scales leave MMLU at chance. Our lightweight post-training pipeline converts an existing checkpoint to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours, a fraction of the cost of learned ternarization, and leads every post-training ternary method at matched or lower memory-resident bits on perplexity, zero-shot accuracy and MMLU, most widely on knowledge. A sparse second ternary plane placed by a per-unit Fisher saliency keeps the matmul multiplication-free and recovers what ternary loses first: at 8B, a fraction of a bit returns about half the MMLU that conversion costs, well ahead of random or Hessian-based placement at equal bits.

title: Fisher Information and Support Complexity of Gaussian Mixtures
abstract: We study lower bounds on the Fisher information of Gaussian location mixtures and their applications to estimation problems. First, for a discrete mixing distribution, we derive a universal positive-semidefinite lower bound on the Fisher information matrix in terms of the Rényi entropy of order two. For a mixing distribution supported on $K$ points, this bound scales as $\log(K)/K^2$, improving by a logarithmic factor on the support-size dependence obtained from Stam's inequality. We then develop dimension-aware trace bounds using classical Sobolev inequalities. These bounds are expressed in terms of Sibson's $α$-mutual information and yield the scaling $K^{-2/n}$ in dimension $n$. A complementary bound involving the $α$-mutual information of order $1/2$ is obtained using the sharp Young convolution inequality. The derived inequalities are further specialized to rotationally invariant mixing distributions supported on discrete spherical shells. In this setting, an intrinsic-dimensional bound on Sibson mutual information leads to lower bounds on the Fisher information in terms of the number of occupied shells. As applications, we study least favorable priors for bounded Gaussian mean estimation. In the scalar case, we show that the least favorable prior on $[-R,R]$ has at least $Ω(R\sqrt{\log R})$ support points and that each of its probability masses is of order at most $1/R$. In the vector case, we show that the number of occupied shells grows at least linearly with $R$. Finally, Brown's identity and the I-MMSE relationship are used to translate the Fisher-information inequalities into upper bounds on the MMSE and mutual information.

title: Score Mismatch and Set-Constrained Sampling in Zero-Shot Conditional Discrete Diffusion
abstract: Discrete diffusion models have become a powerful framework for modeling complex discrete distributions across a range of applications. While theoretical convergence guarantees depend on consistency between the target and training distributions, such a case rarely holds in practice, making score mismatch a central challenge in discrete diffusion sampling. This is particularly relevant to zero-shot conditional generation, where a model trained on the unconditional distribution is directly reused at inference time to sample from a conditional target distribution. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical analysis for score-mismatched discrete diffusion models and derive a general KL divergence upper bound that clearly identifies the additional bias caused by such a mismatch. Our analysis covers partial-observation constraints, including text infilling, sentence completion, and more general coordinatewise set constraints. Specifically, we analyze the classical Conditional SEDD sampler and show that it can incur a bias term that scales with the dimension, vocabulary size, and compatibility. Based on this analysis, we propose a Randomized Hard Clamping (RHC) sampler for coordinatewise set constraints. We show that the assignment probabilities can be expressed exactly by the unconditional scores with absorbing rate. Finally, numerical and real-data experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RHC sampler.

title: ControlFlow3D: Distilling Multi-View Knowledge into Latent Flow Matching for Point Cloud Upsampling
abstract: Point cloud upsampling is essential for 3D applications but remains challenging due to sparse, under-constrained observations. Multi-view images can resolve geometric ambiguity, but existing multi-modal methods do not fully exploit visual cues. We propose ControlFlow3D, a framework that distills knowledge from pretrained foundation models into a lightweight generation network during training, enabling strong performance without multi-view images available at test time. Specifically, our method performs conditional flow matching in a structured latent space defined by a frozen 3D encoder. Multi-view image tokens and 3D latent tokens are jointly clustered into shared prototypes via unsupervised soft KMeans; the resulting prototypes guide the flow trajectory through velocity control and are aligned by a consistency loss that progressively transfers image knowledge into the base network. A Mamba-based geometry decoder then maps latent features to dense coordinates with linear complexity. We also construct ShapeNetPU, a 35K-object multi-modal benchmark that is 31 times larger than prior datasets. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and its strong generalization capability.

title: EVA-Cap: Optimizing Audiovisual Video Captioning via Event-Centric Alignment
abstract: Recent advances in Omni Language Models (OLMs) provide a unified solution for audiovisual video captioning. Nevertheless, existing approaches predominantly treat captioning as an unstructured text generation process, neglecting the inherent semantic structure of videos and leading to suboptimal fine-grained audiovisual alignment. To bridge this gap, we propose EVA-Cap, a novel framework that decomposes captions into atomic audiovisual events and transforms unstructured text supervision into event-centric alignment. We train EVA-Cap via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a self-curated dataset, EVA-Data, which is built with event-centric quality control. During the GRPO phase, the model is explicitly optimized against three event-centric alignment targets: global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap significantly outperforms existing methods in event-centric evaluation (e.g., +9.0% average gain on ChronusAV), while achieving competitive performance on general audiovisual captioning benchmarks (e.g., +3.3% on WorldSense).

title: LAMP: Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors for Training-Free Few-Shot Vision-Language Adaptation
abstract: Few-shot adaptation often relies on an encoder's final global representation, leaving complementary information in intermediate layers underused. Combining these features is challenging because their dimensions can differ and their usefulness varies across tasks. We propose LAMP, Layerwise Adaptive Mixing of Predictors, a training-free framework that combines global and regional information from multiple encoder layers. A single forward pass per view supplies all descriptors. Global and support-calibrated regional kernel predictors independently fit the same label residuals. Labeled validation data select their mixture in class-score space, preserving native feature dimensions without learned projections. LAMP-F further adapts text-anchored class prototypes, using a cached response to update the fixed-kernel residual predictions exactly. Experiments cover eleven datasets and ViT and ResNet backbones. LAMP achieves state-of-the-art mean accuracy among the compared published training-free ResNet-50 methods at 4, 8, and 16 shots, reaching 78.73% at 16 shots. Averaged across five support budgets, LAMP improves over a paired global-feature-only baseline by 1.14 and 1.59 percentage points on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; LAMP-F raises these gains to 1.96 and 2.54 points. LAMP-F reaches 16-shot accuracies of 83.57% and 79.10%, respectively. Controlled experiments identify multi-layer integration as the main source of improvement and examine pooling, calibration, validation labels, and computational cost. These findings show that combining layer-specific predictions can exploit complementary features from frozen encoders to improve few-shot classification.

title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream task at hand? We study this question through stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, which can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance. We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources. We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy.

We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources. We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy.

title: The Lagrangian Structure of Cost-Penalized Active Feature Acquisition
abstract: Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) sequentially selects features to maximize predictive accuracy under an acquisition budget. A natural heuristic greedily maximizes Expected Information Gain minus a cost penalty, EIG(j|x_S)-lam*c_j (EIG-Cost), but its theoretical guarantees are unclear. We provide an a-posteriori certificate decomposing the gap to the optimal hard-budget policy into a budget-slack term and a greedy-suboptimality term Del_lam. The certificate is computable when the penalized optimum is tractable; on small heterogeneous-cost instances, we verify it exactly, finding Del_lam near zero across 4,000 solved cases. On the large clinical task, Del_lam is not computable, so the decomposition is diagnostic rather than a numerical guarantee. Our analysis identifies EIG-Cost as one-step greedy optimization of the Lagrangian relaxation of expected-cost AFA, with lam as its dual multiplier. For equal costs, we prove Del_lam <= exp(-gam*I(Y;X_[d])), where gam is the submodularity ratio, yielding a structural guarantee in the near-submodular regime. Supporting results establish an adaptive chain-rule identity showing that cumulative stepwise EIG optimizes transcript information, and prove that A -> I(Y;X_A) need not be submodular, even for jointly Gaussian variables. This rules out a direct Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher bound; naive Bayes restores submodularity. We also bound the randomization gap between hard-budget and expected-cost optima, analyze sensitivity to dual-multiplier error under local smoothness, and derive a conditional CVAE generator-shift bound given a bound on forward predictive KL. We treat this KL as a diagnostic quantity, not as a transform of training loss. Experiments cover synthetic Gaussian settings, AFA benchmarks, and clinical differential diagnosis on MIMIC-IV. On MIMIC-IV, EIG-Cost achieves macro-F1 0.180 +/- 0.012 at a $30 budget, using 6.6% of full-panel cost.

title: Learning to Reason with Selective Internal Feedback
abstract: Reinforcement learning from internal feedback can improve language models without ground-truth answers or external verifiers. However, confidence and correctness can diverge during training, and continued optimization of average self-certainty can increase confidence while degrading reasoning accuracy. We introduce SIF, a reinforcement learning method that combines comparative reward construction with selective policy updates. SIF compares ranked token-level self-certainty profiles across multiple windows and peers, assigning positive rewards only when both levels of voting provide sufficient support. Sample and group level filtering determines which responses contribute to policy optimization. Experiments on three backbones across 12 mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks show that SIF's final checkpoints achieve higher average accuracy than the best-validation checkpoints of Intuitor and Vigor, with a gain of 4.71 percentage points over Intuitor on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B. Further analyses show better retention of accuracy during continued optimization, while test-time training experiments demonstrate sustained improvements with as few as four rollouts per prompt.

title: TEM: Temporal State Tracking Memory for Large Language Model Agents
abstract: An agent's memory must remain useful as information changes across conversations. A new fact may replace an earlier value without making that value irrelevant to a later question. We present Temporal State Tracking Memory (TEM), a training-free framework for tracking these changes. TEM stores facts as versioned records linked to their sources. It retrieves relevant versions, places them in source order and labels historical records before passing the evidence to the answer model. Event memory and original dialogue turns provide details missing from structured facts. We evaluated TEM on 420 questions drawn from 600 sessions involving 60 personas. Across four open-weight models, key-entity hit rates reached 75.71-97.62% overall and 96.67-100.00% on the historical-residence subset. Adding historical labels to otherwise identical, source-ordered facts increased overall hit rates by 17.14-55.95 percentage points. The evidence was compact: 94-118 tokens per answer, or 48.75-56.73% less than session-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A further evaluation on 1,540 LoCoMo questions tested hybrid memory under a fixed evidence budget. TEM exceeded session-aware RAG with both backbones; conservative score differences were 7.92 and 10.58 percentage points. The results support preserving fact versions and exposing their temporal status to the generator when answering questions about repeatedly updated information.

title: Baselines and Score Centering in Policy Gradient Estimation
abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a widely used approach to post-training large language models. In a typical implementation, learning is off-policy: The policy generating the responses differs from the policy being trained because of training-inference mismatch or policy staleness in asynchronous training. This discrepancy is commonly addressed by importance sampling, whose ratio is usually regularized in practice through truncation, masking, or clipping. Under regularized importance sampling, the importance-weighted policy gradient is no longer invariant to constant shifts in the reward. This invariance is recovered by using the covariance between the reward and the importance-weighted score as the estimand, which coincides with the policy gradient when the ratio is not regularized. This note develops this covariance perspective for both sequence-level and token-level importance sampling. The covariance perspective reveals the roles of the group-mean baseline and score centering in policy gradient estimation. Both perform centering in covariance estimation, but they differ in the mean being subtracted: The group-mean baseline uses a sample mean, whereas score centering uses a population mean. The two lead to distinct unbiased covariance estimators with different variances. Whether both forms of centering should be used simultaneously depends on whether importance sampling is applied at the sequence level or at the token level. With sequence-level importance sampling, score centering adds no benefit once the group-mean baseline is used; with token-level importance sampling, using the group-mean baseline without score centering generally introduces bias when the importance ratio is regularized.

title: Evaluation of LLMs in Answering Questions: A Case Study on POSCOMP
abstract: Several studies have investigated Large Language Models’ (LLMs) ability to answer questions from national educational assessments. However, specialized domains such as databases remain underexplored. Furthermore, current literature lacks a comprehensive analysis of how multimodal capabilities affect accuracy and stability across multiple runs. This study aims to fill these gaps by evaluating the accuracy and stability of five modern LLMs in solving 25 database questions from POSCOMP, using API requests, with hyperparameter control and five independent runs per configuration. The models investigated were GPT-5 Nano, GPT-5.4, Grok 4.1 Fast, Gemini 3 Flash Preview, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, considering both LaTeX and image inputs. Additionally, we applied non-parametric statistical tests to evaluate the significance of performance differences between these input modalities. The results show that Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview demonstrated the best overall performance, outperforming the other models in both accuracy and consistency across runs, while GPT-5 Nano and Grok 4.1 Fast exhibited significant performance degradation under image inputs. Finally, the findings reinforce the importance of API-based evaluations with multiple independent runs to analyze not only the accuracy but also the reliability of responses generated by LLMs in technical domains.

title: Ontology-Enriched GraphRAG: A Case Study in Portuguese Geoscience Question Answering
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) in Question-Answering (QA) tasks. However, traditional text-based retrieval may prove insufficient in specialized domains, such as geoscience, where critical information is highly interconnected and distributed across complex concepts, relations, and interpretative descriptions. While Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) addresses part of this limitation by structuring evidence into entity-relation graphs, it remains susceptible to terminological inconsistencies, synonyms, and domain-specific variants. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a controlled empirical study evaluating ontology-enriched GraphRAG for Portuguese geoscience QA. We systematically compared four generation strategies: LLM-only, textual RAG, standard GraphRAG, and ontology-enriched GraphRAG. The ontology-driven approach grounds text-extracted entities in formal reference ontologies using a cascading matching strategy that starts with embedding-based semantic similarity, followed by URI-based, label-based, and alternative-label-based matching. Evaluated across semantic, lexical, contextual, and graph-level metrics, our results confirm that external retrieval is indispensable, as retrieval-based strategies outperform the LLM-only baseline. Textual RAG achieved the strongest lexical overlap, while ontology-enriched GraphRAG achieved the highest Correctness, Completeness, and Contextual Recall. GraphRAG provided stronger grounding and question alignment, as reflected by higher Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy. Beyond these answerand context-level gains, the most substantial effect of ontology enrichment was structural, driving a substantial expansion in graph semantic coverage, graph size, and matching rate. These findings suggest that ontology grounding acts primarily as a powerful enabling mechanism for semantic representation; however, its impact on answer quality depends on retrieval, subgraph selection, and prompt construction.

title: Adaptive Switching between Self-Supervision and Collaborative Supervision in Multi-Agent Learning Systems
abstract: Multi-agent learning systems can exploit information generated by individual agents or benefit from supervision provided by other agents. Self-supervision enables an agent to learn from intrinsic structures, prediction consistency, and internally generated training signals, whereas collaborative supervision enables agents to exchange, evaluate, and utilize supervisory information from their peers. Although both paradigms have received considerable research attention, relying exclusively on either mode can introduce limitations. Self-supervision may reinforce systematic errors or provide insufficient corrective information, while collaborative supervision may increase computational costs, communication overhead, and exposure to unreliable supervisory signals. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Collaborative Supervision (ASCS), a multi-agent learning framework that dynamically switches between self-supervision and collaborative supervision according to the estimated learning state of each agent. Rather than enforcing a fixed supervision strategy throughout training, ASCS treats the supervision mode as an adaptive decision variable. The switching mechanism considers predictive uncertainty, temporal learning progress, inter-agent disagreement, supervisory reliability, and collaboration costs. Each agent can independently select self-supervision, request or receive collaborative supervision, or temporarily abstain from unreliable supervisory information. The framework further incorporates a cost-sensitive switching objective, reliability-weighted supervisory signals, and a hysteresis mechanism to reduce unstable mode transitions. This paper formalizes the framework, presents its optimization objectives and operational algorithm, and develops a research methodology for evaluating its effectiveness against fixed-mode and non-adaptive baselines. The proposed framework is intended to support classification, representation learning, multimodal learning, distributed learning, and multi-agent systems in which supervisory information can be generated internally or obtained from peer agents. Its principal research hypothesis is that adaptive supervision can provide a more favorable balance among learning quality, robustness, and computational efficiency than a permanently fixed supervision mode. Empirical validation is required to determine the conditions under which this hypothesis holds.

title: Adaptive Reasoning and Collaborative Reasoning Between Self-and-Other Models: A Unified Framework for Adaptive Switching, Integration, and Metareasoning
abstract: Reasoning systems often operate according to a predefined computational strategy. A system may rely on autonomous reasoning within an individual model, or it may coordinate multiple models through information exchange, distributed inference, mutual criticism, and collaborative synthesis. However, neither autonomous reasoning nor collaborative reasoning is universally optimal across all tasks, computational conditions, and uncertainty levels. Autonomous reasoning may be efficient but insufficient for problems requiring complementary knowledge or independent verification. Collaborative reasoning may improve coverage and error detection but introduce communication costs, coordination delays, correlated errors, and unnecessary computational overhead. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self-and-Other Model Reasoning Framework (ASOM-R), a conceptual framework for dynamically selecting, switching between, and integrating self-reasoning and collaborative reasoning within a higher-level Self-and-Other Model paradigm. The framework is not defined as a large language model or a particular neural network architecture. Instead, it represents a model-level organization in which a system can reason through its own internal processes, coordinate with other models, or combine both modes according to task-dependent conditions. The framework introduces a metareasoning controller that estimates the expected value of additional reasoning, evaluates uncertainty and disagreement, considers computational costs, and selects an appropriate reasoning configuration. Four operational modes are specified: autonomous reasoning, collaborative reasoning, sequential hybrid reasoning, and parallel hybrid reasoning. The framework further defines a switching policy, a cost-sensitive decision objective, a convergence criterion, a model-interaction protocol, and an experimental evaluation methodology. The central hypothesis is that adaptive selection can achieve a more favorable balance among accuracy, reliability, computational cost, and response latency than systems restricted to a single reasoning mode. This hypothesis requires empirical validation and is not presented as an established experimental result.

title: Analisis Sentimen Willow Project Pengeboran Minyak Besar-Besaran di Alaska Bisa Hancurkan Bumi Menggunakan Metode Naive Bayes Berdasarkan Komentar di YouTube
abstract: Tujuan dari penelitian ini adalah untuk melakukan analisis emosional terhadap proyek pengeboran minyak besar-besaran di Alaska yang dikenal sebagai "Proyek Willow". Metode Naive Bayes digunakan untuk memperkirakan opini berdasarkan komentar di platform YouTube. Studi ini mengkaji pendapat dan perasaan masyarakat terhadap proyek tersebut, dengan fokus pada kemungkinan dampak negatif terhadap lingkungan. Hasil analisis sentimen ini dapat memberikan wawasan yang lebih mendalam mengenai dukungan atau penolakan masyarakat terhadap proyek pengeboran minyak. Implikasi dari hasil penelitian ini dapat digunakan sebagai dasar pengambilan keputusan berkelanjutan dalam pengembangan proyek energi skala besar, dengan mempertimbangkan tanggapan masyarakat dan kekhawatiran yang diungkapkan dalam komentar di platform online.

title: Constructing a Multi-modal Intelligence Audit System Based on Biosensors and Deep Fusion
abstract: This study presents a multimodal intelligence audit system based on biosensors and deep fusion for safety, quality, and compliance assurance in biomedical systems. The system aligns heterogeneous evidence from physiological biosensor streams, electronic health records, medical-device logs, clinical text, images, audio, and procedural video, and then applies an attention-enhanced long short-term memory (LSTM) network for temporal anomaly detection. A constrained agentic layer converts model evidence into traceable audit tasks, retrieves supporting records, checks predefined clinical-engineering rules, and drafts reports subject to human approval. On the available enterprise audit dataset (12,600 samples), the implementation reduced total audit time by approximately 80% and achieved 96.0%-99.0% task-level accuracy. The biomedical extension is presented as a method-transfer framework rather than as a claim of completed clinical validation: patient-level evaluation, calibration, and prospective clinical testing remain required. The work therefore contributes a reproducible alignment interface between multimodal sensing, temporal fusion, and human-governed audit agents for biomedical engineering and clinical operations.

title: Content associations with answer selection and engagement in supply chain community question answering
abstract: Community question-answering platforms are important ecosystems for knowledge sharing, yet research on what makes an answer best or a question engaging has often focused on either individual lexical features or broad topics. This exploratory study examines both levels in Yahoo! Chiebukuro, asking which nouns and semantic noun clusters are associated with best-answer selection and question engagement. We analyze a large corpus of questions and answer-tier posts collected under the keyword logistics, using an offline machine-translation pipeline with manually validated noun-level fidelity. Best-answer selection is modeled with conditional logistic regression within question threads, controlling for answer length, order, and question-answer noun overlap. Engagement is modeled in two stages: whether a question receives any response and, conditional on receiving one, how many responses it attracts. Operational logistics nouns such as distribution, warehouse, and center are associated with best-answer selection, whereas broader civic and infrastructure nouns such as car, tax, and shinkansen are associated with higher engagement. At the cluster level, most semantic noun clusters are associated with best-answer selection, while the clusters associated with response likelihood and response volume are largely distinct. These findings reveal differentiated content-outcome profiles across answer and question levels and provide a domain-wide descriptive map of engagement and answer selection in logistics-related cQA discourse.

title: Making every stage of medical device document assessment with large language models deterministic
abstract: To show that a medical device complies with regulation, experts judge whether documents and records meet each requirement and record the judgment for others to verify. For each assessment item that experts define, large language models could prepare a preliminary assessment: a label such as Satisfied or Not satisfied, a reason and quoted evidence. We sent fourteen commercial deployments of such models (seven models from three providers, through six routes) the same request repeatedly, with the deterministic sampling settings each accepted; every deployment returned differing assessments for at least one request, and in twelve the label changed. Reducing reasoning where the interface allows it did not reduce the variation, and prompts of retrieved passages removed it only for the smallest models. The same open-weight model was reproducible or not depending only on how it was served. A pipeline we built to be deterministic at every stage -- text extraction and optical character recognition (OCR), chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval and inference -- returned byte-identical output at each stage across reruns, interruptions, edits, machines of one graphics processing unit (GPU) model and days, for blood glucose meter and infusion pump documents. OCR, embedding and approximate retrieval varied when their own serving was not made invariant, and outputs changed with the GPU model and with the inference engine's scheduling settings, which therefore belong in the recorded configuration. End-to-end determinism is achievable and gives a testable basis for audit and change control.

title: Emotion Is Not External Knowledge: Internal Attention Signals for Affective State Reasoning
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts, at the answer position, the content tokens these heads already attend to; both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model's own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks.We evaluate on ECC and GoEmotions across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Across settings, SIAB improves prompt-matched baselines by up to +10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and +5.5 on GoEmotions. Combined with PASTA-style external supervision, it achieves up to +13.84 accuracy points and +12.51 macro-F1 points, while mechanistic analyses trace the gains to sparse, emotion-enriched heads and show that layer proximity affects additivity.

title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
abstract: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with DeepSeek V3.2 and from 50 to 53 with Kimi K2.7 Code. On disjoint ALFWorld unseen tasks, success rises from 50.75% to 71.64%. Across archived architecture-snapshot transitions, the median code-change ratio is 4.4%. These results support fine-grained execution evidence as a basis for localized, in-place memory-architecture evolution.

title: REKI: Registering Knowledge in VLAs
abstract: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.

title: Mine, Sample, Render: Test-Time Diversity Alignment Of Generative Models
abstract: Modern generative models produce high-quality individual outputs but struggle to sample diversely, even when explicitly instructed to do so. We introduce MINE-SAMPLE-RENDER (MSR), a test-time approach that externalizes the diversity into an explicit, corpus-derived sampling procedure. Our pipeline (i) mines an interpretable categorical schema from a corpus of real artifacts and supplies statistics for sampling; (ii) samples attribute configurations from the corpus-derived statistics; (iii) uses a generative model purely as a conditional renderer of a sampled configuration. Across weather report generation, user simulation, webpage design, text-to-image generation, and agent-generated 3D assets, we evaluate the diversity and output quality of MSR-guided generation and show that MSR improves alignment with corpus distributions and diversity of generated outputs.

title: Sci$Π$vot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct Sci$Π$vot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while Sci$Π$vot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.

title: Generalization Guarantees of Randomized Block Coordinate Descent for Nonconvex Learning
abstract: Randomized block coordinate descent (RBCD) is a popular optimization algorithm for many large-scale machine learning problems. The existing theoretical analysis of RBCD mainly focuses on its convergence behavior from an optimization perspective, while its generalization behavior remains less understood for nonconvex problems. In this paper, we establish high-probability generalization guarantees for RBCD with nonconvex objectives. In the general nonconvex setting, we derive bounds on the gradients of both empirical and population risks, requiring only standard smoothness assumptions. With polynomially decaying step sizes, we tune the iteration number to balance optimization and generalization, thereby quantifying how early stopping leads to the optimal convergence rate for the population gradients. In the gradient-dominated setting, we provide bounds in terms of functional suboptimality, which nearly match the optimistic rates in convex and low-noise settings. Finally, we develop dimension-independent bounds for loss functions of a specific structure, making the generalization guarantees applicable to high-dimensional problems.

title: Dimension-Free PAC-Bayes Generalization for Deep Neural Networks via Dirichlet Processes
abstract: Classical PAC-Bayesian generalization theory places prior distributions over Euclidean parameter space $Θ\subseteq \mathbb{R}^D$, causing relative entropy to scale with network dimension $D$. For modern overparameterized neural networks where $D \gg n$, this parameter-counting dependency yields vacuous generalization bounds ($> 1{,}000\%$). In this work, we resolve this barrier by shifting prior specification from internal parameters to the non-parametric space of data distributions $\mathcal{M}_1(\mathcal{Z})$ via a \textbf{Dirichlet Process (DP)}, $\mathcal{DP}(α, F_0)$, inducing parameter distributions through push-forward measures under the learning algorithm. By the Data Processing Inequality, parameter-space relative entropy is strictly bounded by the data-space DP divergence, which we evaluate in exact closed form using Digamma functions. The resulting PAC-Bayesian certificate is strictly invariant to network parameter count $D$, width, and depth. On intrinsic $d^*$-dimensional submanifolds, optimal partition scaling achieves the minimax non-parametric rate $\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/(d^*+2)} \sqrt{\ln n})$. title: Writability and the Pathway: A Controlled Study of Knowledge Injection into Addressed Memory
abstract: Addressed conditional memory provides a local surface for post-hoc knowledge injection, but a successful write need not transfer to a new question or preserve untargeted behavior. This study combines a controlled GPT-2 comparison with production-memory experiments on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Newly initialized modules attached to frozen GPT-2 are tested in a 2 x 2 design: row-only versus row-plus-projection updates, each with or without fixed module-residual anchoring. All arms reproduce 50 trained completions in each of three sampling seeds. Natural-question target-string hits average 5.3% for both row-only arms, 28.7% for unanchored projection updates, and 22.0% with anchoring, while strict answer scores remain zero. Anchoring lowers measured drift; lexical hits do not establish entity-specific retrieval. In the archived Qwen experiments, gradient writes make the designated first answer token top-ranked for 132 independently reset targets, comprising 93 new promotions and 39 already top-ranked targets. A separate matched 24-target comparison gives 13 new promotions with Adam versus two with SPSA at equal iteration counts but unequal computational procedures. An 80-row case includes saved continuations and a replay record, while reformulations bound its scope. Six DeepSeek zero-order cases yield one new target-token promotion and one regression. These results support bounded writing feasibility and separate trained expression, question-form behavior, and preservation; first-token rankings do not establish complete-answer success or universal conditions for writable memory.

title: Bootstrapping Text Anomaly Detection with LLM-Generated Weak Supervision
abstract: Text anomaly detection is challenging because anomalous instances often share vocabulary and surface form with normal data, making them hard to distinguish without semantic understanding. Semi-supervised methods can significantly outperform unsupervised baselines, but rely on labeled anomalies that are rarely available in practice. LLMs encode rich semantic knowledge that can approximate human judgments, yet using them directly as detectors is costly at inference time and sensitive to prompt design, while generating synthetic outliers risks distribution mismatch with real anomalies. We propose a different strategy: treating a compact, locally deployed LLM as a noisy annotator over real data. The LLM scores a small subset of unlabeled documents once at training time, producing weak labels that refine a sentence encoder via contrastive fine-tuning and train a lightweight downstream detector — without cloud APIs, human annotation, or curated anomaly datasets. Across four datasets spanning two languages and two tasks, the approach recovers up to 79% of the gap to oracle upper bounds while using 14–91× fewer labeled anomalies. We further identify three failure modes that explain when LLM-generated weak supervision succeeds or breaks down.

title: Vidya Syl: A syllable division algorithm for Brazilian Portuguese adhering to the Common Orthographic Vocabulary of the Portuguese Language
abstract: Syllabification is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) applications, particularly in readability assessment through metrics such as the Flesch Index. This paper presents Vidya Syl, a new syllabification algorithm implemented in Java, developed in compliance with the Brazilian section of the Common Orthographic Vocabulary of the Portuguese Language, known as VOC. The methodological approach consisted of augmenting a rule-based algorithm grounded in phonological and graphical rules with morphological and orthographic rules, until it became compliant with VOC. The experimental results demonstrate improvements in both accuracy and lexical coverage.

title: Implementation of Neural Networks for Direction Control of DC-Motor
abstract: In this paper, a neural network was implemented to control the direction of a DC motor. In this context, attention was paid to the field of artificial intelligence related to neural networks. The network targeted for training is small in size, and the tasks required of it are limited and include the direction of rotation of the DC motor axis, which has two directions (clockwise rotation or counterclockwise rotation). DC motors are used in applications such as robotics and automated manufacturing. It is a rotary actuator or linear actuator that allows control of linear direction. The main purpose of this work is to provide a clear view of the importance of using neural networks in the control field. In this study, the ANN is trained by the back-propagation algorithm, and a multilayer neural network is composed to implement the controller that controls the operation of the model using the back-propagation learning algorithm that regulates the function of the DC motor system. It was noticed that changing some parameters such as weights, learning rates, number of hidden layers, or number of nodes can enhance the output and generate the proper control of the direction.

title: SYNTRA
abstract: Code release accompanying the paper Self-improving data synthesis enables scalable adaptation of embedding models (Zucan Lyu, Rui Tang, Jianlyu Chen, Peisheng Jin and Defu Lian), arXiv:2610.14730. SYNTRA generates training data for fine-tuning embedding models from an unlabelled corpus and a few query–document examples. It refines its query-generation and relevance-labelling instructions from feedback on small trial runs, then reuses them for large-scale production. title: Recursive Priced Falsification: Asymmetric Trials with a Forecast-Scored Planner for Autonomous Discovery
abstract: Autonomous discovery loops, in which language-model agents improve a design against an automatic evaluator, spend most of their effort on ideas that fail. We argue that such a loop should be built so that a failure is cheap and a success is not capped, and that the part that decides what to try should be scored like everything else. We introduce recursive priced falsification, an agentic topology that does both. It is an arrangement of agent roles, what each role may read, the gates between them and a record they share. Instruments measure the incumbent design, scouts write priced cards from that map, a pricer runs the cheapest test that could end a card, a builder builds what survives, and a breaker with a fresh context tries to break each claim. What moves between the roles is a trial: a forecast written before a run, the result that would end the idea, and the idea's price in the currency of the objective. Each trial is an asymmetric bet: a stake that is small and known before the run, against a gain that the stake does not cap. Trials are ranked by expected gain per unit of stake, not by their chance of success. The method is recursive: the loop applies it to itself. The loop arrived at its own arrangement of roles this way during the run: it began as a hub, priced candidate roles against its own record, and adopted the arrangement after running it once as a trial, with a forecast written first. The planner that ranks the trials is forecast-scored: it commits to a forecast in every task, every report lists what the task got wrong, a red team attacks its closed directions, and the loop revises its own procedure from its logged mistakes. We give the optimality conditions behind the price map and the ranking rule, an ordering rule for an evaluation cascade, and a rule for which comparison can decide that a change is exact. We implemented the topology in Pensieve, our research harness, and ran it for six days on a live public benchmark for quantum circuit optimisation, with other agent harnesses improving the same circuit under the same evaluator. The best score fell by 5.73% in 42 accepted entries. The loop produced 70.8% of that fall in 17 entries, took the top of the benchmark twelve times, and made the only two steps above 1% by any system (1.45% and 1.04%). The benchmark as a whole moved twelve times as fast during the run as in the five weeks before it (0.99% a day against 0.083%), and fell back to 0.063% a day when the loop stopped. Its trials paid in the way the design predicts. The median trial cost 50 minutes of one worker and kept nothing; the mean trial earned 0.03% of the score, the size of the median accepted entry of the other systems. Ten of 133 trials hold 79% of the loop's points, and the largest of them cost one builder 63 minutes. Trials beat the odds written for them (46% against 30%) and returned 1.6 times the size forecast for them. What paid was a capped loss against an open gain: the largest gains came from trials given about even odds, not from long shots. The loop revised its own procedure during the run, after each of 67 logged mistakes; after the full topology was in place, 1 of 12 builds kept nothing, against 10 of 35 before. We present it as an autonomous research loop and not as recursive self-improvement: the foundation model is frozen, and no revised loop was tested against its predecessor under a matched budget. The comparison with the other systems is observational and has no ablation. All research was carried out by the agents; a human operator set the goal, approved actions with effects outside the loop and sent occasional directions on strategy.

title: Who Spoke Next Is Not Who Should Have: What Zero-Shot Failure on Multi-Party Turn-Taking Benchmarks Measures, Why the Human Reference Sits Beside the Models, and What Would Show That Knowing When to Speak Must Be Trained
abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. An assistant that joins a group conversation has to decide, at every pause, whether to take the floor. Two 2026 benchmarks report that language models prompted zero-shot make this decision badly and that fine-tuning repairs it, and both conclude that knowing when to speak is learned rather than emergent. Other 2025-2026 work reports the opposite pattern on neighbouring tasks: untuned models beat human subjects at predicting the next speaker in meetings, and the predictive uncertainty of a model with no task training locates speaking opportunities better than either prompting or fine-tuning. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the disagreement is about three different quantities that one speak-or-silent score mixes: discrimination (whether a system speaks more often where speaking is appropriate), operating point (how often it speaks at all, which depends on costs and a role the prompt never states), and the target (whose behaviour the label records). Re-weighting the one published human reference to the benchmark's own category mix, the author finds that human annotators would score about 57 percent balanced accuracy on the Friends portion, below the best zero-shot model's 60.5. What fine-tuning visibly adds is a shift in operating point and agreement with the corpus on the one category where humans and corpus disagree; whether it also adds discrimination, the published results do not identify. The paper gives a decision procedure for what a speak-or-silent result licenses and specifies the score-based, cost-stated and panel-labelled measurements that would show whether the capability is missing. The argument covers text-transcript evaluation most firmly; for full-duplex speech models the evidence is thinner and is treated separately.

title: "CF-Boost: Leakage-Free, Calibrated Focal-Loss Hybrid Boosting for Liver Disease Prediction"
abstract: "Liver disease causes about two million deaths peryear, yet machine-learning studies on the widely used IndianLiver Patient Dataset (ILPD) often report accuracies that cannotbe reproduced. We identify the underlying gap: ILPD contains13 duplicate records and a 71\/29 class imbalance in which thehealthy class is the minority. Common pipelines that oversamplebefore splitting leak test information, while leakage-free standardclassifiers collapse toward the majority class (specificity oftenbelow 0.30). We propose CF-Boost, a calibrated focal-loss hybridboosting framework that combines (i) clinically-informed featureengineering (De Ritis ratio, ALP\/ALT pattern, conjugatedbilirubinfraction, LFT abnormality burden), (ii) a LightGBMbranch trained with an analytically differentiated class-balancedfocal loss, (iii) a class-balanced linear branch, and (iv) a stackingmeta-learner with Youden-optimal threshold calibration, all fittedstrictly inside training folds. On ILPD (n=570) and the UCI HCVdataset (n=608) with 10\u00d75-fold cross-validation and correctedresampled t-tests, CF-Boost reaches a balanced accuracy of 0.694and 0.976, respectively. It is significantly better than 11\/14 and8\/14 baselines, is the best-calibrated imbalance-aware model onboth datasets (lowest Brier score overall on HCV), and uses fewerthan 1.5k parameters with sub-millisecond latency. A leakageaudit shows that oversampling before the split inflates RandomForest accuracy on ILPD from 0.673 to 0.837."

title: An Interpretable Neural Generalized Linear Model for Insurance Pricing
abstract: This article proposes a modeling framework, termed the Actuarial Neural Generalized Linear Model (AN–GLM), which integrates a traditional generalized linear model (GLM) with a deep neural network (DNN). The goal of the proposed algorithm is to increase modeling flexibility while maintaining interpretability, and to offer a practical, implementable alternative to the relatively simple pricing models commonly employed by insurance practitioners, whose predictive accuracy is often limited. The proposed framework consists of two components: a knowledge-based component and a data-driven component. The model is designed to automatically discover a well-performing model specification without sacrificing interpretability, allowing both expert-driven structure and data patterns to jointly determine the Poisson claim frequency. We provide theoretical support for the proposed architecture, establishing conditions under which the proposed model is statistically sound. Furthermore, we assess its empirical performance through extensive simulation experiments and a real world insurance application using policy level data. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides both theoretical and practical contributions to the actuarial science field by offering an interpretable, robust, and empirically validated alternative for modern insurance pricing.

title: FALCON: FPGA-Accelerated Latency-Certifiable Occupancy Networks for Camera-Based Autonomous Driving
abstract: A perception system that must brake for a pedestrian does not need a low average latency. It must deliver an answer before the deadline on every frame, the worst case included. Commodity edge accelerators optimize the mean through dynamic scheduling, OS jitter, thermal throttling, and contention, so their per-frame latency can be measured but not bounded. We build FALCON, a camera-based 3D occupancy front-end on the AMD Kria KR260, an embedded FPGA drawing 4.3 W idle and up to 6.6 W under inference, and make the latency guarantee layered and explicit: programmable-logic (PL) compute is cycle-bounded analytically; inference is a measured envelope over 100k-frame traces; and a watchdog enforces output delivery, publishing the previous output flagged stale when a frame is late. The deadline runs use a fixed-work proxy of six ResNet-50 DPU inferences per frame, not the full occupancy network: across three 100k-frame enforced runs, all 300k proxy frames delivered an output within the 100 ms deadline plus at most 10.2 ms, the worst of the three runs. The full six-camera FlashOcc pipeline composes to about 1.3 s per frame on the board and is not yet a 10 Hz system. The two operations the DPU cannot run, a view-transform gather and a bilinear resize, become fixed-trip-count PL IPs numerically matched to their software references. evidence.abstract: A perception system that must brake for a pedestrian does not need a low average latency. It must deliver an answer before the deadline on every frame, the worst case included.
