title: Learning and Forecasting Multiscale Spatiotemporal Epidemic Dynamics with Lagrangian-Eulerian Graph Neural ODEs
abstract: Accurate medium- to long-range epidemic forecasting requires extrapolating high-dimensional, heterogeneous and nonstationary dynamics from partial observations. Yet hybrid models often leave implicit which observations inform which epidemic processes and how learned graph interactions modify system state. We introduce LE-EpiGNODE, which replaces generic message passing with process-specific, mechanism-guided neural operators: age-contact information drives Lagrangian infection generation, whereas mobility drives conservative Eulerian population transport within a structure-preserving universal differential equation. We evaluated LE-EpiGNODE across 14 controlled synthetic mechanisms spanning time-modulated, state-dependent, nonlinear and coupled dynamics, three complementary COVID-19 settings, 21 comparator models and five targeted ablations. Forecasting gains tended to become more pronounced at longer horizons; at the longest horizon, LE-EpiGNODE achieved the lowest WMAPE in all three real-world datasets, reducing error by 17.7-40.0% relative to the best baseline. Controlled ablations linked these gains to the Lagrangian-Eulerian decomposition and process-aligned priors, while synthetic ground truth showed that learned operators and induced state fluxes track known generating dynamics. These results support mechanism-organized graph neural dynamics as a route to reliable long-horizon extrapolation with directly testable, process-level mechanistic interpretation beyond trajectory accuracy.

title: Inferência Textual Zero-Shot em Português: Especialização Linguística vs. Raciocínio Explícito em Modelos de Linguagem Compactos
abstract: Este trabalho investiga a capacidade inferencial de modelos de linguagem de pequeno e médio porte (até 9B de parâmetros) na tarefa de Inferência em Linguagem Natural (NLI) em português brasileiro, em regime estritamente zero-shot. Partindo da definição formal de acarretamento como preservação de condições de verdade, uma relação dedutiva na classificação peirceana [Peirce 1932], comparamos modelos especializados em português (Sabiá, Bode, Gaia) com modelos multilíngues equipados com mecanismos explícitos de raciocínio e destilação de conhecimento (Qwen3, Gemma 2, Ministral 3) no ASSIN 2 e em um dataset sintético controlado, fundamentado em acarretamento por inclusão lexical (hiponímia / hiperonímia). Os resultados indicam que raciocínio explícito e destilação são mais decisivos do que adaptação monolíngue isolada, e que acurácia elevada no ASSIN 2 pode superestimar a competência inferencial ao confundir similaridade distribucional indutiva com preservação dedutiva de condições de verdade.

title: STAB: A Complexity-Ladder Framework for Evaluating Local LLMs as Autonomous Agents
abstract: O uso de Large Language Models (LLMs) em sistemas agênticos locais enfrenta desafios críticos de consistência e confiabilidade, especialmente em hardware de consumo. Este trabalho apresenta o protocolo STAB, uma metodologia de avaliação em escada de complexidade (S1→S4) combinada a um protocolo de estabilidade temporal para diagnosticar falhas em agentes on-premise. Avaliamos oito modelos de quatro famílias (Qwen, Gemma, Llama e Mistral) em servidor com GPU NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12 GB VRAM). Os resultados revelam que as falhas agênticas originam-se predominantemente na camada de instrução e decisão contextual, e não na capacidade bruta dos modelos. title: Structural AI Interpretability: A Geometry‑First Framework for Hallucination Detection, Drift Analysis, and Silicon‑Level Governance — Preprint v1.0 (Architecture Edition)
abstract: Structural AI Interpretability: A Geometry‑First Framework for Hallucination Detection, Drift Analysis, and Silicon‑Level Governance — Preprint v1.0 (Architecture Edition) introduces a geometry‑first framework for understanding, detecting, and preventing hallucination in modern reasoning systems. Rather than treating hallucination as a behavioral anomaly or a failure of factual recall, this work demonstrates that hallucination is a geometric collapse event within the latent manifold. When stability invariants are missing—curvature bounds, modal adjacency constraints, spectral‑state manifolds, operator‑field typing rules, and non‑harm boundaries—expressions drift away from grounded semantics, collapse surfaces emerge, and hallucination becomes inevitable. This preprint presents a complete structural pipeline: 1. LeanHallucinationGuard (Semantic Enforcement Layer) A deterministic enforcement enclave that intercepts syntactic mimicry, semantic drift, operator‑field confusion, modal instability, and spectral mismatch before execution. GitHub repository: https://github.com/Borealiscodes/Lean-Hallucination-Guard LeanHallucinationGuard enforces geometric invariants, humanitarian non‑harm constraints, modal adjacency rules, operator‑field typing, and deterministic abort logic. It transforms hallucination from an opaque failure mode into a structured geometric event with measurable telemetry. --- 2. Geometric Interpretation Toolkit (Analytic Layer) A suite of geometric operators—spectral bundles, collapse‑surface classifiers, modal‑truth lattices, holonomy drift tensors, spectral mismatch metrics, and stability envelopes—that make hallucination measurable, reproducible, and scientifically analyzable. These operators quantify drift, detect collapse surfaces, identify spectral degeneracy, and reveal modal instability. They provide the analytic backbone for geometry‑first interpretability. --- 3. ProvenanceShield (Silicon‑Level Governance Layer) A hardware‑rooted governance framework built on AMD SEV‑SNP and Intel TDX attestation. ProvenanceShield ensures that all reasoning occurs inside a cryptographically attested enclave with immutable invariants, verified operator provenance, and deterministic execution boundaries. GitHub repository: https://github.com/Borealiscodes/ProvenanceShield ProvenanceShield prevents unverified symbolic assemblies, pseudo‑formal constructs, and hallucinated operators from escaping into execution—especially in safety‑critical environments. --- 4. CMR Telemetry Artifact (Drift‑Collapse Case Study) The preprint analyzes the Compressed Manifold Reachability (CMR) manuscript (Reed 2026) strictly as a hallucination‑geometry telemetry artifact, not as a validated robotics algorithm. CMR exhibits syntactic mimicry, semantic drift, spectral mismatch, modal adjacency violations, collapse surfaces, and drift‑tensor accumulation. These failure modes illustrate how missing invariants allow plausible‑looking but structurally inconsistent derivations to form. --- 5. Appendices and ASCII‑Stable Diagrams The record includes extensive appendices: - Lean falsification excerpts - collapse‑surface ASCII diagrams - drift‑tensor ASCII visualizations - spectral bundle ASCII illustrations - ProvenanceShield schematic All diagrams are ASCII‑stable and accessible, ensuring compatibility with screen readers and long‑term archival formats. --- Purpose of This Zenodo Record This Zenodo deposit provides: - the full Structural AI preprint - all appendices - ASCII‑stable diagrams - enforcement code (LeanHallucinationGuard) - governance code (ProvenanceShield) - geometric toolkit operators - provenance materials - drift‑collapse case study documentation Together, these components form a unified, deterministic, invariant‑preserving architecture for grounded reasoning, geometric interpretability, and silicon‑level governance.

title: Adaptive Machine Learning in Non-Stationary Environments: A Systematic Review of Concept Drift Detection and Mitigation in Data Streams
abstract: The proliferation of high-velocity data streams in domains such as IoT, cybersecurity, and financial technology has exposed the limitations of static machine learning models. When the underlying data distribution changes over time, a phenomenon known as concept drift occurs, leading to severe model degradation `[1]`. This paper presents a systematic review of 29 foundational and contemporary studies on concept drift detection and adaptation. We categorize detection mechanisms into statistical, window-based, and model-based approaches, while evaluating adaptation strategies ranging from dynamic ensembles to lightweight incremental learning `[16]`. Furthermore, we address compounding challenges, including class imbalance and the emergence of novel classes `[2]`, `[30]`. By synthesizing recent advancements, this review provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing robust, real-time, and resource-efficient streaming machine learning systems `[27]`

title: GeoQA-PG: a knowledge system-guided retrieval-augmented framework for geographical question answering in Pedogeography
abstract: Geographical Question Answering (GeoQA) is transitioning from traditional rule-based and retrieval-based approaches to intelligent paradigms driven by large language models. As an important component of geographic artificial intelligence, GeoQA aims to provide reliable and interpretable geographic knowledge services. However, existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods remain inadequate for geographic questions requiring structured knowledge and coherent logical reasoning. To address these challenges, this study proposes GeoQA-PG, a question answering framework for pedogeography. Specifically, a tree-network knowledge system is constructed by integrating a hierarchical knowledge framework with a fine-grained knowledge graph. Building on this knowledge system, a dual-channel retrieval mechanism, named SoilKnowRAG, is developed. It combines text and graph retrieval to mitigate knowledge fragmentation. Based on GeoQA-PG, SoilGPT is implemented and evaluated using a question answering dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that SoilGPT significantly outperforms baseline models with comparable parameter scales on both objective and subjective tasks, while the comparative evaluation of SoilKnowRAG further confirms its effectiveness compared with other RAG methods. Overall, GeoQA-PG provides a transferable framework for knowledge-driven GeoQA and advances the intelligent representation, reasoning, and services of geographic knowledge.

title: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate differential diagnoses for complex cases, but a useful second opinion must also be factually grounded, clinically coherent, actionable, and safe. We developed a multidimensional benchmark using 300 diagnostically resolved NEJM--MedQA cases: 110 for physician reference ratings and Judge calibration and 190 for held-out evaluation. Eight single-model pipelines generated independent role-specific opinions and interactive-consilium reports under free-form and structured clinical-reasoning conditions. A physician-calibrated LLM Judge evaluated 3,040 final reports and the corresponding structured primary-role outputs. Model identity separated report quality more strongly than response format. Structured final reports had higher overall mean scores in seven of eight model pipelines, with their clearest advantage in management (2.740 vs. 2.436). Compared with the structured pre-consilium primary-role opinion, the complete structured synthesis had higher pooled scores across all five shared criteria, with the largest increases in problem prioritization, factual grounding, and reasoning coherence. GPT-5.6-Sol led every evaluated component and reached consensus in the fewest review rounds. These findings show that the benchmark can distinguish model capability, the contribution of multidisciplinary synthesis, criterion-specific effects of response structure, deliberation dynamics, and inference requirements within one common-case evaluation.

title: Progress Reward Model for Reinforcement Learning via Large Language Models
abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long-term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning-based approaches often depend on pre-defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low-level control policies, while reward-based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high-level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask-oriented, fine-grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low-level reward generation, inspired by potential-based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM-based planning and reward methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/deng-ai-lab/PRM4RL.

title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
abstract: Language embeddings are increasingly used in recommenders to represent item content, but their privacy risks remain poorly understood. We study whether item embeddings can reveal item identities when an adversary has access to auxiliary item text from external sources. We show that a simple cosine-similarity attack can recover item identities with high mean reciprocal rank across language models and candidate-set settings on two real-world datasets. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's partial information overlaps with the victim representation, but it also persists through semantic alignment between independently sourced descriptions. We further show that item leakage can propagate to user re-identification from sparse ratings. Finally, we evaluate obfuscated descriptions as a mitigation and find a clear leakage-utility tradeoff.

title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
abstract: Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output-level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165--228x faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.

title: Early-stage mortality prediction for ICU-admitted liver disease patients
abstract: Liver disease carries substantial mortality risk, and the early-stage prediction of mortality for patients initially admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) could effectively support clinical decisions about their care. Prior hospital records are an established source of predictive signal for in-hospital mortality, but they vary in depth and length and are absent for patients without prior admissions, which most existing approaches do not accommodate. This thesis develops three approaches that progressively change how prior clinical history is represented for in-hospital mortality prediction at 24 hours after ICU admission in liver disease patients, using the MIMIC-IV database. The first adapts a process-mining framework with an XGBoost classifier, taking clinical scores calculated by the first 24 hours after ICU admission and process-mining history features as input. The second replaces the tabular classifier with a deep-learning model that encodes physiology over the first 24 hours after ICU admission as a temporal sequence, combined with the same process-mining history representation. The third keeps this 24-hour physiology sequence but replaces the process-mining history with a knowledge-graph representation grounded in the Unified Medical Language System, where the relational structure is enriched by LLM-extracted triples from prior discharge notes, and a graph attention network over the resulting graph contributes to the mortality prediction. Our results show that the first approach improves on the existing process-mining baseline under matched evaluation. The second approach does not improve predictive performance over the first, but its multi-branch design allows the contribution of each input source to be measured separately. The third approach also covers patients without prior admission records, a subgroup excluded by the first two approaches, without a loss of performance relative to patients with recorded history.

title: Arabic HPSG grammar for LKB — frozen release 5f (grammar, lexicon, test suite, treebank selection and evaluation scripts)
abstract: An HPSG grammar of Modern Standard Arabic in TDL for LKB-FOS 5.6, in which inflection, derivation, agglutination and syntax are stated in one type hierarchy: 721 types, 280 inflectional, 27 derivational, 31 broken-plural and 31 agglutination rules, 57 syntactic rules, a lexicon of 32,581 entries (canonical lexicon, Arramooz-derived lexicon, treebank supplement, particles, 3,666 listed broken plurals). The archive also contains the test suite of 347 sentences with expected results, the UD Arabic-PADT selection (sentences of at most twelve words) with the deterministic dev/test split, the conversion, scoring and feature-comparison scripts, the derivation-tree exports of every run reported in the accompanying article, the neural baseline scores and the result reports. This is the frozen release evaluated in the article “A Unified HPSG Morpho-Syntactic Grammar for Modern Standard Arabic” (submitted to Language Resources and Evaluation). See LISEZMOI.md for the layout and the commands that regenerate each table.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Knowledge Integration and Cross-Model Knowledge Integration in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve problem-solving by integrating knowledge within individual agents and exchanging knowledge across multiple agents. However, these two processes are often treated as separate capabilities or are embedded in collaboration strategies that do not explicitly optimize the transition between them. Continuous cross-agent knowledge exchange may introduce communication overhead, redundant information, conflicting representations, and unnecessary coordination, whereas exclusive reliance on internally available knowledge may prevent agents from exploiting complementary knowledge held by other agents. This paper proposes Adaptive Self-and-Cross-Model Knowledge Integration (ASCKI), a general framework that enables multi-agent systems to adaptively switch between self-knowledge integration and cross-model knowledge integration according to task requirements, knowledge completeness, uncertainty, information conflict, expected integration benefit, and communication cost. Self-knowledge integration combines information available within an individual agent, including its internal representations, accumulated experiences, retrieved memories, and intermediate conclusions. Cross-model knowledge integration combines information originating from multiple agents or models to construct a more comprehensive collective knowledge representation. The proposed framework introduces a shared decision mechanism, a dual-mode integration architecture, an adaptive switching policy, and a knowledge-quality feedback loop. The switching policy evaluates whether continued internal integration is sufficient or whether external knowledge exchange is likely to provide additional value. The framework is model-agnostic and can be applied to heterogeneous or homogeneous agents, including language-model-based agents, distributed reasoning systems, autonomous learning systems, and knowledge-intensive multi-agent applications. This paper formalizes the framework, presents its operational algorithm, identifies research hypotheses, and develops an empirical evaluation protocol. Rather than claiming experimentally established improvements, it establishes a testable research direction for reducing unnecessary collaboration while preserving the benefits of collective knowledge integration.

This paper formalizes the framework, presents its operational algorithm, identifies research hypotheses, and develops an empirical evaluation protocol. Rather than claiming experimentally established improvements, it establishes a testable research direction for reducing unnecessary collaboration while preserving the benefits of collective knowledge integration.

title: Adaptive Learning and Collaborative Self-Adaptive Learning Between Self-and-Interaction Models: A Unified Framework for Adaptive Mode Switching
abstract: Learning systems often face a fundamental design choice between adapting independently and adapting through collaboration. Independent adaptation allows a model to preserve its autonomy, exploit its own experience, and avoid unnecessary coordination costs. Collaborative adaptation allows multiple models to exchange information, learn from complementary experiences, coordinate their adaptation strategies, and respond to problems that exceed the capabilities of individual models. Relying exclusively on either mode may be inefficient in dynamic environments, particularly when the relative value of independent and collaborative learning changes over time. This paper proposes a unified framework for adaptive learning and collaborative self-adaptive learning between Self-and-Interaction Models (SIMs). In this framework, a Self-and-Interaction Model is conceptualized as a model-level computational entity that supports self-directed processing and interaction with other models. It is not defined as a large language model, nor does it require any particular neural architecture. The proposed framework enables a model to operate in a self-adaptive learning mode, a collaborative self-adaptive learning mode, or a transition process between the two. Mode selection is governed by an adaptive controller that considers learning progress, uncertainty, prediction error, knowledge complementarity, interaction cost, resource availability, and the expected value of collaboration. The framework formalizes model states, local adaptation, collaborative adaptation, mode selection, information exchange, and adaptive switching through a unified mathematical formulation. It also introduces mechanisms for selective collaboration, confidence-aware information integration, adaptive interaction frequency, and safeguards against harmful information transfer. A research methodology is outlined to evaluate the framework against fixed-mode and non-adaptive switching baselines across heterogeneous and changing environments. Because the framework has not yet been experimentally validated in this paper, its expected benefits are presented as testable hypotheses rather than established results. The proposed approach provides a general research foundation for investigating how self-directed and collaborative adaptation can coexist within a unified model-level learning architecture.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Rewarding and Mutual-Rewarding Processes in Self-and-Mutual Models: A General Framework for Model-Level Reward Coordination
abstract: Reward mechanisms determine how computational systems evaluate their behavior, allocate learning resources, and improve their future decisions. Existing research has investigated intrinsic rewards, self-generated feedback, reward shaping, individual incentives, shared rewards, and cooperative multi-agent learning. However, a general framework for adaptively switching between self-rewarding and mutual-rewarding processes at the level of a distinct class of Self-and-Mutual Models remains an open research direction requiring formalization and empirical investigation. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self–Mutual Reward Coordination Framework (ASMR-CF) for Self-and-Mutual Models (SMMs). The proposed framework treats self-rewarding and mutual-rewarding as complementary operational modes rather than mutually exclusive system designs. In self-rewarding mode, a model evaluates its own candidate actions, predictions, plans, or computational outcomes using internally available evidence and task-relevant evaluation criteria. In mutual-rewarding mode, multiple models exchange evaluations, assess one another's contributions, and construct reward signals that account for cross-model consistency, complementary expertise, and shared objectives. An adaptive controller estimates the relative utility of these modes and determines whether to continue self-rewarding, activate mutual-rewarding, or combine both mechanisms. The framework is designed to operate independently of any particular model architecture, learning algorithm, or reward-generation technique. It introduces a formal representation of model-level reward coordination, an adaptive mode-selection mechanism, safeguards against self-confirming reward errors and mutual-reward manipulation, and an experimental protocol for evaluating the proposed approach. Unlike approaches that assume a fixed reward structure, ASMR-CF explicitly treats the choice of reward mechanism as a decision that can change over time. The paper establishes a conceptual and methodological foundation rather than claiming experimentally demonstrated improvements. Its central research question is whether adaptive coordination between self-generated and mutually generated reward signals can improve performance, reliability, efficiency, and robustness compared with fixed reward strategies.

title: Directional Complexity of SIGReg with Anisotropic Gaussian Targets
abstract: Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) aligns learned representations with an isotropic Gaussian target along random one-dimensional projections. LeJEPA establishes finite-direction guarantees because the rotational symmetry of this target makes every direction identical. Structured representations, however, require anisotropic targets that vary across directions. We prove that while target anisotropy preserves the geometric approximation rate, directional complexity depends on the target’s centered spectral moments and spectral endpoints. We show empirically that across targets with matched condition numbers, spectral shape governs direction budgets. These budgets scale with the target’s spherical Dirichlet energy and initial slicing-gradient variance, while its leading angular harmonic couples directly to directional sampling error. To eliminate this quadratic coupling, we introduce Orthogonal Directional Slicing (ODS), which draws complete random orthonormal frames that enforce exact second-moment balance. While ODS reduces gradient variance across all conditions, it does not reliably lower direction budgets, as higher-degree angular harmonics dominate directional complexity. Reducing this complexity therefore requires canceling these higher-order harmonics, rather than simply drawing more directions.

title: Mitigating Hallucination Cascades in Multi-Agent Systems via Consensus-Aware Knowledge Verification
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex task automation. However, these systems suffer from a critical vulnerability: hallucination cascade, where erroneous information generated by one agent propagates through the system and is amplified by downstream agents. We propose Dynamic Consensus Auditing (DCA), a novel framework that introduces a lightweight audit agent to monitor inter-agent message flows. DCA combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with uncertainty quantification based on semantic entropy to detect potentially hallucinated content. When high-uncertainty messages are detected, DCA triggers a peer review mechanism where multiple agents vote on the validity of the information. Experiments on HotpotQA, TriviaQA, and MuSiQue benchmarks demonstrate that DCA reduces error propagation rates by 42.5% (relative reduction) on average compared to baseline multi-agent systems, with a token overhead of 15.3% (averaged across datasets). Our results suggest that, in the context of multi-hop question answering with three-agent pipelines, consensus-aware verification provides a practical balance between reliability and computational efficiency in multi-agent collaboration.

title: AI Versus Knowledge Workers
abstract: The case concerns the consulting firm LegalExpert, whose main activity is advising companies on the generation of new business, as well as the development of a strategy for implementation. The case describes the tensions that arise when incorporating AI into organizational management, especially in knowledge-intensive firms, as well as the practical considerations to be taken into account when initiating this type of intervention. This study contributes to a better understanding of the incorporation of AI in the specific cultural and political context of an organisation. Likewise, this article contributes to a better understanding of the advances of AI in emerging economies, as well as the particularities of its implementation in the specific context of these countries.

title: Name-Bias in Large Language Models
abstract: Names carry demographic indicators such as age, gender, and race, which makes them a subtle but strong target of bias in large language models (LLMs). In this work, we present an evaluation of name-based bias across 6 local large language models spanning multiple providers and parameter scales. Using a fill-in-the-blank task, we prompt these models to choose between pairs of first names drawn from U.S. Social Security Administration datasets and a race classification dataset by Rosenman et al.. Our experimental de- sign isolates age and gender effects through balanced name pairings and sentence templates that share a fixed syntactic structure. Across 300,000 local LLM responses, we find consistent and measurable name bias. Models prefer names that are less stereotypically male, older, popular, and white. Furthermore, we find that name-bias is highly sentence-dependent, but not more than associated stereotypes, and gender is the most significant bias, followed by age, name popularity, and race. Our results demonstrate that name-based bias remains pervasive even in local LLMs, highlighting the necessity for standardized evaluation methods and mitigation strategies.

title: Loss-independent time-delay estimation via Hong-Ou-Mandel photon bunching detection
abstract: In this work we study the application of two-photon correlated quantum states for high-precision time estimation. To achieve this, photon pairs were fed into a Hong-Ou-Mandel polarization interferometer to generate N00N entangled states with $N = 2$. Two- and four-detector schemes were considered, and the achievable time estimation precision of each was studied, with particular emphasis on the system's Fisher information in each case. Our results reveal that using a four-detector scheme, enabling the measurement of both coincidence and photon-bunching terms, achieves the maximum precision given by the quantum Fisher information, without the need of characterizing system losses. We also show that correlations between repetitions arise due to systematic errors, limiting the precision enhancement that can be obtained by increasing the number of repetitions. Taking these correlations into account, we show that the four-detector scheme outperforms the two-detector scheme in the precision of time-delay estimation. With the experimentally determined calibration uncertainties, the four-detector scheme improves the dispersion by a factor of 2 for the repetitions performed, reaching up to a factor of 4 as both schemes approach their systematic floors.

title: Robust Covariance Estimation for Entry-wise Contaminated and Partially Observed Data via Expectation Maximization Algorithm
abstract: Robust covariance estimation under entry-wise contamination and missing data is challenging in various signal processing applications. Under the Student-$t$ model, observation-level reweighting induces a uniform attenuation across samples, which can lead to cumulative information loss even when most coordinates remain informative. The alternative Student-$t^*$ model enables coordinate-wise robustness, but its E-step is not available in closed form. We extend inference for the Student-$t^*$ model to incomplete observations through a stochastic approximation EM (SAEM) algorithm operating on a reduced latent space: stochastic updates of the coordinate-wise scales are combined with Rao-Blackwellized Gaussian conditional moments, which avoids explicit sampling of latent Gaussian variables while preserving a likelihood-based framework. Experiments on synthetic and real sensor data show a lower Fisher-Rao error than Gaussian, Student-$t$, imputation-based and detect-then-estimate estimators at moderate to high outlier rates under diffuse contamination.

title: Policy-Aligned Predictive Verification for Adaptive VLA Action-Chunk Execution
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate action sequences that reduce repeated inference, but deciding how much of each sequence to execute is critical to task success. Existing adaptive methods make this decision using generation stability or prediction agreement, yet these signals do not establish whether executing a candidate prefix preserves the ability to complete the task. We introduce a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. Rather than using future prediction to generate actions, our method evaluates existing proposals in the VLA's internal task-conditioned representation space. To learn local judgments from terminal task outcomes, we combine trajectory-level survival supervision with a localization prior that preserves useful behavior within failed rollouts. The resulting validity scores guide execution-horizon selection. Evaluations with pi_0 and pi_0.5 across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success-query trade-offs. These findings point toward a different role for future prediction in robotics, using it to assess how far to trust a policy's proposed actions rather than to generate new ones.

title: Curupira: Arquiteturas Híbridas Transformer-BiLSTM para Detecção de Discurso Ofensivo em Português Brasileiro
authors: Patricia Medyna Lauritzen de Lucena Drumond
abstract: Este trabalho apresenta o Curupira, estudo empírico controlado de arquiteturas neurais para detecção de discurso ofensivo em português brasileiro sob protocolo metodológico rigoroso: split treino/validação/teste honesto, cinco sementes aleatórias, controle explícito de capacidade paramétrica e teste de significância via bootstrap pareado. Oito configurações são avaliadas no OLID-BR, cobrindo quatro ordens de magnitude em parâmetros. Os resultados devem ser interpretados para este conjunto de dados e regime de treinamento, e indicam cinco achados principais: (i) o desempenho se concentra próximo de Macro-F1 = 0,70, com o BERTimbau (110M de parâmetros) superando um híbrido Transformer→BiLSTM leve (350K) em 4,3 pontos; (ii) a atenção global produz ganho estatisticamente significativo sobre uma BiLSTM equiparada em capacidade; (iii) aumentar a capacidade neural não melhora o desempenho no cenário avaliado; (iv) a ordem de composição importa, com Transformer→BiLSTM superando BiLSTM→Transformer em 6,3 pontos; (v) codificação posicional senoidal sobre embeddings congelados degrada substancialmente o desempenho, reduzindo o Macro-F1 de 0,66 para 0,26.

title: Adaptive Self-Search and Collaborative Search in Self-and-Mutual Models: A Unified Framework for State-Dependent Search Switching
abstract: Search is a fundamental process through which computational systems explore possibilities, discover information, identify solutions, and improve their internal representations of a problem. Existing approaches include independent search, population-based search, multi-agent collaborative search, and adaptive combinations of different search strategies. However, these approaches do not necessarily provide a unified, model-level framework in which autonomous search and collaborative search are treated as two complementary operating modes of a broader model architecture. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self-Search and Collaborative Search Framework for Self-and-Mutual Models (ASCS-SMM). The framework conceptualizes Self-and-Mutual Models as a model-level architecture that supports both independent exploration and interaction among models. Self-search enables a model to explore a search space using its own internal state, experience, hypotheses, and available computational resources. Collaborative search enables multiple models to exchange information, compare candidate solutions, divide search tasks, and jointly explore regions that may be difficult to investigate independently. A state-dependent switching mechanism determines when the system should continue self-search, initiate collaborative search, maintain collaboration, or return to independent exploration. The proposed framework integrates search-state estimation, uncertainty assessment, progress monitoring, resource allocation, diversity preservation, collaboration utility estimation, and switching-cost management. It is intended to be applicable to optimization, scientific discovery, planning, knowledge exploration, and other computational systems without requiring a specific model architecture or learning paradigm. This paper develops the conceptual foundations, formal definitions, mathematical formulation, operating procedure, evaluation hypotheses, and experimental design of the framework. As a conceptual proposal, its effectiveness and novelty relative to the complete existing literature remain to be established through systematic review and empirical evaluation.

title: Fundamentals of Digital Signatures
abstract: This chapter presents the core principles of digital signatures and explains why they are fundamental to secure digital systems and blockchains. We learn how digital signatures provide data integrity, authenticity, non-repudiation, and how these properties reinforce each other. The chapter explains the working mechanisms of major signature schemes, including RSA and ECDSA, with attention to correctness, security assumptions, and computational efficiency. It then shows how digital signatures operate in blockchain systems, covering the UTXO model, account-based design, and recent advances such as SegWit, Taproot, deterministic signing, and signature aggregation. We can examine key properties required in blockchain settings, including privacy, scalability, and resistance to forgery. The chapter concludes with a comparative overview of representative schemes such as multisignatures, blind signatures, ring signatures, threshold signatures, and EdDSA.

The chapter concludes with a comparative overview of representative schemes such as multisignatures, blind signatures, ring signatures, threshold signatures, and EdDSA.

title: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking
abstract: Neural watermarking systems are typically trained as tightly coupled embedder-detector pairs and implicitly assume static deployment. In real-world deployments, embedders and detectors are frequently updated and selectively decoupled for security and versioning purposes, which can break detection in previously embedded content and, more critically, increase false-positive rates on embedders that a given detector is intentionally not intended to recognize. In this paper the concept of backward compatibility in zero-bit audio watermarking is formalized. A training framework is proposed that pairs a new detector with a sequence of frozen legacy embedders (its legacy chain), using a performance-weighted sampling strategy so that the detector retains accuracy across all earlier versions. This coupling, while necessary for backward compatibility, is shown to induce an embedder-collapse effect that catastrophically degrades the true negative rate (TNR) against out-of-chain embedders. To counteract this, a Angular Diversity Loss (ADL) is introduced that explicitly forces each new embedder to occupy a distinct region of the output space. The combined approach restores near-perfect TNR with no measurable cost to detection accuracy or perceptual audio quality.

title: Rethinking Successive Rejects Algorithms
abstract: In the best-arm identification problem, an algorithm adaptively selects arms to find the arm of the largest mean reward. Successive Rejects (SR) is a simple fixed-budget best-arm identification algorithm that eliminates one candidate arm at each phase. At first glance, SR seems to have limited adaptivity, since it follows predetermined phase lengths. However, for Gaussian arms with common variance, SR's worst-instance error exponent normalized by the popular complexity measure $H_1(P)$ is optimal up to a constant factor, which partly explains why SR's performance is competitive compared with state-of-the-art adaptive sampling algorithms. In this paper, we extend the framework of SR by optimizing its predefined schedule of phase lengths. We formulate phase-schedule design as an optimization problem for the normalized error exponent. Then, we introduce a version of SR with the optimized schedule, which we call $H_1$-balanced Successive Rejects ($H_1$-SR). This schedule is optimal within the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count schedules. For Gaussian arms with common variance, $H_1$-SR achieves at least $11/12$ of the optimal normalized rate over all adaptive algorithms for every $K\ge2$, and this approximation ratio converges to one as $1-O(1/\log K)$ as $K\to\infty$. This is a significant improvement over original SR, whose corresponding fraction of the optimal normalized rate converges to $1/4$. Finally, experiments on ten synthetic instances and two dataset-derived Gaussian benchmarks compare the optimized schedule with original SR at finite horizons. They show substantial gains on many instances while also exposing a regime in which more aggressive early elimination is costly.

title: ManiFusion: Unlocking the High-Throughput Generation via Superposition in Manifold Space
abstract: Diffusion models achieve high-quality image generation but remain computationally expensive due to iterative denoising across many timesteps. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation.

title: DLOSAC: Joint Spatial-Geometric Image Estimation via Delaunay-Guided Local Optimization RANSAC
abstract: Reliable image geometric estimation from noisy matching points is typically addressed using RANSAC, often combined with local optimization to refine inliers and model parameters. However, existing paradigms are predominantly residual-centric; even heuristic attempts to enforce spatial uniformity suffer from a sequential, two-stage nature that inherently decouples distribution optimization from geometric refinement, preventing an effective trade-off. In this paper, we propose DLOSAC, a local optimization framework that jointly incorporates both geometric consistency and spatial distribution information. We begin by constructing a Delaunay triangulation over candidate inliers to explicitly encode neighborhood topology. The geometric module introduces an edge-based consistency metric to evaluate geometric errors, while the spatial module derives distribution descriptors from triangle areas and edge attributes to quantify the clustering of inliers. Finally, we combine edge-based geometric constraints, spatial distribution regularization, and traditional point-level geometric constraints to improve the quality of geometric parameters. Extensive experiments on six publicly available real-world datasets, covering three types of geometric estimation tasks, achieve state-of-the-art performance.

title: Fine-grained prosody control in speech synthesis
abstract: Human speech tells us more than written text. Through prosody, we can add information either about ourselves and how we are feeling, or about the lexical content and how it should be understood. Text-to-speech (TTS) models have achieved highly controllable lexical content, evidenced by highly intelligible output. The same level of prosody control has not yet been achieved. We can choose what is being said, down to the phoneme, but not exactly how it is said in terms of the pitch, loudness, timing, and voice quality. This is crucial for creating speech that is appropriate in a given context and fulfils end-user needs. Current approaches commonly rely on utterance-level style embeddings or natural language descriptions, or training on massive amounts of data for greater prosody variation. They do not allow direct prosody adjustments to reflect the context or personal preference of the TTS user. Some TTS systems explicitly model a subset of the acoustic correlates of prosody. In theory, these predictors allow fine-grained control, but this is left implicit and rarely tested in-depth. The models appear easy to control, but is it straightforward to use this control mechanism and add prosodic information about the content or speaker? In this thesis, we investigate the FastPitch model as an exemplar of the current approach to fine-grained control. We examine its controllability in the context of replicating prosody from a reference recording by explicitly extracting acoustic correlates of prosody and transforming them into targets for the model. This approach to prosody control is called voice puppetry. Using reference speech for control is intuitive, but brings additional considerations. Is it possible to achieve fine-grained control across domains and speaker differences, as well as acoustic features? We first explore whether FastPitch is responsive to changing the predicted acoustic features independently. Results show that the model responds to target changes in two out of three acoustic features, although the targeted values are not produced perfectly in the output. Additional experiments indicate that different reference speakers lead to different controllability success. If the acoustic features cannot be calculated reliably, it affects target calculation and consequent prosody generation. In the data used, pervasive creakiness has a bigger impact on (pitch) controllability than speaker gender and accent. The reference utterances in these experiments have prosodic patterns which add topical emphasis to one word in a sentence. Despite imperfect reproductions of the prosody, results show that the additional information is understood by listeners. The second set of experiments focuses on affective prosody. For these, the reference utterances come from multiple emotion-labelled speech datasets and cover a much larger variety of prosody contours. Through analysis of this data, we highlight the limitations of using z-normalisation in the calculation of speaker-normalised pitch values, as well as the limitations of the training data for generating more extreme acoustic values. We propose two methodology updates which help mitigate these issues but also lead to decreased audio quality and intelligibility. We test the emotion transfer from the reference recordings without overly relying on the emotion labels, retrospectively supported by participant comments on the unsuitability of some reference recording labels. When participants are asked to compare model output to the reference prosody, they mostly rate the emotions as 'expressed very similarly'. Finally, we investigate how the controllability success of our voice puppetry approach compares to two alternatives: Daft-Exprt, a similar model to FastPitch but with a built-in reference encoder, and SeedVC, a zero-shot voice conversion model. Both implicitly model prosody from reference recordings, compared to voice puppetry's explicit extraction of acoustic features. Compared to Daft-Exprt and SeedVC, voice puppetry output produces a more faithful prosody contour, especially the pitch trace. Despite the greater objective faithfulness of voice puppetry output, participants in the listening test judge it to have the lowest affect similarity to the reference. Listening test results also suggest that while the voice puppetry quality is noticeably lower, it does produce output with greater similarity to the training speaker. Fine-grained prosody control remains an open research problem. On the modelling side, the acoustic targets are not produced perfectly in model output. On the speaker side, simple transformations such as shifting and scaling are insufficient to translate prosody from one speaker to another. Given some non-parallel data of a reference speaker and a training speaker, it is difficult to define a prosody transformation which retains the training speaker identity, does not lead to a loss in audio quality, and fully encapsulates the prosodic intent. Through our experiments, we identify a series of challenges which complicate fine-grained prosody control in neural speech synthesis, which future models aiming to offer fine-grained control will need to address.
